comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1-C3, C10 regarding optogenetic tool development and validation. Both evaluations find the technical implementation compelling and well-supported without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on claims C11-C20 describing phenotypic distributions across GEF constructs. OpenEval focuses on quantitative evidence (35% retraction, 40% protrusion), while peer reviewers emphasize this as the 'interesting observation' and note functional diversity of RhoGEFs. Peer review also includes C24-C27 (generalizability) in their evaluation.

Agreement on claims C22-C23 regarding spatial independence of phenotypes. OpenEval explicitly discusses the Sankey diagram evidence, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the expression-level dependency without raising concerns. OpenEval also addresses C21 which is not mentioned in peer review.

Both address generalizability claims C24-C27. OpenEval notes minor weaknesses in HeLa cell quantification, while peer reviewers incorporate these claims into their broader acceptance of phenotypic diversity across GEFs without specific critique.

Strong agreement on concentration-dependent phenotypic switch (C28-C30, C108-C109). OpenEval emphasizes the sharp transition at 40 a.u. with large sample size, while peer reviewers state authors 'convincingly show' this relationship but raise a 'major caveat' about global overexpression effects not captured in OpenEval's evaluation.

Agreement on cell state changes (C31-C37). OpenEval highlights convergence of multiple independent measurements (overexpression, cell size, membrane dynamics), while peer reviewers accept the expression-level dependency but express the same 'major caveat' about global overexpression effects.

Perfect agreement on temporal cytoskeletal dynamics (C38-C43). Both accept the high temporal resolution data showing actin and myosin dynamics. OpenEval provides detailed statistical analysis, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the mechanistic explanation without concerns.

Agreement on differential RhoA activation kinetics (C44-C48). OpenEval notes the iRFP biosensor limitation and resulting bias, while peer reviewers accept these findings as key evidence for the mechanism without raising this technical concern.

Agreement on biphasic RhoA dynamics (C49-C51). OpenEval notes the mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the sequestration mechanism at high GEF concentrations.

Agreement on optoPH-induced RhoA inhibition (C52-C55). OpenEval notes variable effects and modest mean response, while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating the sequestration mechanism convincingly.

Strong agreement on mutation experiments (C56-C59). Both evaluations view this as critical genetic evidence. OpenEval emphasizes clear elimination of protrusion phenotype, while peer reviewers state this demonstrates dependence on Rho-binding activity of the PH domain.

Agreement on claim C60 showing optoPH recruitment alone is insufficient. OpenEval explicitly discusses this as establishing need for active Cdc42 activation, while peer reviewers incorporate this into their broader acceptance of the sequestration mechanism.

Strong agreement on GTPase cascade (C61-C68). OpenEval provides detailed discussion of multiple biosensors and temporal patterns, while peer reviewers accept Cdc42 and Rac1 activation as part of the mechanism. Peer review does not explicitly mention C62.
Perfect agreement on pharmacological validation (C69-C71). Both evaluations accept IPA3 experiments as strong causal evidence for Cdc42-PAK pathway role in protrusion without concerns.

Strong agreement on mathematical modeling (C72-C75, C111). OpenEval notes some dynamics not well-captured, while peer reviewers describe it as 'convincing theory' that 'captures well the dynamics' and emphasize the power of combining modeling with optogenetics.

Agreement on UNCERTAIN evaluation for frequency-based control (C77, C112). Both note the extremely low success rate (3/90 cells, 3.3%) raises questions about robustness. OpenEval suggests additional factors not captured by model, while peer reviewers note it works 'in principle but with very limited reproducibility.'

Agreement on mechanistic synthesis (C78-C80, C110). OpenEval notes relative contributions are inferred rather than directly measured, while peer reviewers accept this as the key finding explaining the switch between protrusion and retraction. Peer review also includes C99 in their evaluation.
OpenEval evaluates literature citations (C4-C9) establishing foundation for current work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers implicitly accept this context.
OpenEval evaluates biochemical mechanism citations (C81-C85) from literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Perfect agreement on GEF-specific differences (C87-C93). OpenEval correlates phenotypic behavior with published PH domain properties, while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating 'functional diversity of RhoGEFs' without extensive discussion.

Strong agreement on PRG's physiological context (C94-C98). OpenEval notes apparent contradiction between FRET and biosensor measurements, while peer reviewers emphasize this mechanism provides 'convincing explanation for this conundrum' of RhoA's context-dependent roles. Peer review also includes C118.

Partial overlap on claim C99 regarding protein dynamics and cellular responses. OpenEval discusses comparison to prior work on dynamic encoding, while peer reviewers incorporate this into their summary of the key mechanistic finding.

Partial overlap on claim C118 regarding Rho GTPase biology. OpenEval evaluates this as part of established knowledge citations, while peer reviewers use this context to frame the significance of findings.
OpenEval evaluates methods claims (C103-C107) as clearly documented and appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though methods are implicitly accepted.
